analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators block brand-name drug companies from paying generic rivals to delay cheaper drugs.
analysis.headline: With a Democrat as sponsor and a Republican as cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug maker challenges a brand-name company's patents, the two sometimes settle by having the brand-name company pay the generic company to stay off the market for years. The bill would let the Federal Trade Commission treat such pay-for-delay deals as presumptively anticompetitive, with civil penalties up to three times the value changing hands, and would strip the first generic filer of its 180-day market exclusivity if it cut such a deal. It never moved beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs still under patent, and the insurers, employers, and government programs that pay for prescriptions. The bill's own findings note generics cost 80 to 85 percent less than brand-name drugs, so any delay in generic entry keeps prices high for everyone who takes the drug.

how_it_helps.text: The bill presumes that a patent settlement in which the generic filer receives anything of value in exchange for delaying its generic drug is anticompetitive and a violation, reversing the burden onto the companies to prove the deal is procompetitive.
It imposes a civil penalty on violators of up to three times the value received, and makes the FTC the enforcer, giving the agency dedicated authority over these agreements.
It requires companies to file and certify all related agreements with the FTC within 30 days, closing a gap where side deals could be hidden from regulators.
A generic company that enters a violating settlement forfeits its 180-day first-filer exclusivity period, taking away the prize that made a payoff deal attractive in the first place.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to pay a generic competitor to stay off the market and thereby extend their monopoly profits. Generic manufacturers would lose the payments they receive for agreeing to delay.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts early-market-entry licenses, litigation-expense payments up to $7.5 million, and covenants not to sue, but its blanket presumption against any settlement involving value could also chill settlements that genuinely benefit consumers, since companies must prove procompetitive benefits by clear and convincing evidence rather than having a court weigh the deal's merits.

Some antitrust scholars argue certain negotiated settlements, particularly those with an agreed generic entry date, can deliver cheaper drugs sooner than years of litigation, and a rigid presumption may push companies to litigate patent cases to the end instead of settling at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main downside is a risk of chilling some legitimate settlements, softened by explicit exemptions for entry-date licenses, capped litigation-expense payments, and covenants not to sue. The upside is direct: every year a pay-for-delay deal adds to a drug's monopoly is a year patients, insurers, and government programs pay brand-name prices for something that costs 80 to 85 percent less as a generic.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 12, 2017 for herself and Senator Grassley, a Republican, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day.
The action history shows no further activity of any kind, no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote, for the remainder of the 115th Congress.

The bill's stated purpose was to stop agreements in which brand-name companies share their monopoly profits with potential generic competitors to protect the monopoly, which the findings describe as more profitable for both companies than competition.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies keep the option of paying generic rivals to stay off the market, and generic companies keep collecting those payments, so the prices patients and insurers pay stay higher for longer.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought to ban compensation for delayed generic entry.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.role: Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but, as the committee chairman who controlled its agenda, never scheduled a markup or vote and let it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored it and a top Republican cosponsored it, and because no vote ever took place there is no recorded party split, only bipartisan sponsorship followed by committee inaction.

industries.note: Pay-for-delay settlements let these companies extend patent monopolies by paying generic challengers to wait, splitting monopoly profits with them. The bill makes that arrangement a violation with penalties up to triple the value exchanged.

Generic companies have collected substantial payments for agreeing to stay off the market. The bill ends that income stream and strips the first-filer exclusivity of any generic that signs a violating deal, though the generic-making industry as a whole benefits from more early entry.

industries.industry: Health insurers, employers, and government health programs
industries.note: Generic drugs cost 80 to 85 percent less than brand-name versions, so faster generic entry directly lowers what insurers, employers, and federal programs, which already cover over 40 percent of retail prescription drug spending, pay.
